en: The Sūtra of the Girl Sumati, translated by the Upāsaka Zhi Qian of Yuezhi during the Wu Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.
At that time, the World-Honored One was together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus.

At that time, there was an elder named Anāthapiṇḍada, who possessed abundant wealth and many treasures—gold, silver, precious gems, mother-of-pearl, agate, pearls, amber, crystal, and lapis lazuli—as well as elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, male and female slaves, and attendants beyond counting.

At that time, in the city of Pūrṇabhadra, there was an elder named Pūrṇadhana, who was also exceedingly wealthy and possessed of many treasures—cat’s-eye, agate, pearls, amber, crystal, and lapis lazuli—and whose elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, male and female slaves, and attendants were beyond counting.

This householder Anāthapiṇḍada and I have been close friends since our youth, cherishing and respecting one another without ever forgetting that bond. Furthermore, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada always possesses many tens of millions of precious treasures and goods for sale in the city of Pūrṇavardhana, which he entrusts to the householder Pūrṇa to manage and protect;

likewise, the householder Pūrṇa also possesses many tens of millions of precious treasures and goods for sale in the city of Śrāvastī, which he entrusts to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada to manage and protect.
At that time, Anāthapiṇḍada had a daughter named Sujātā, whose countenance was so exquisite and her complexion as radiant as a peach blossom that she was a rarity in the world.
Then, on account of some minor business, the elder Pūrṇa arrived at Śrāvastī and went to the house of the elder Anāthapiṇḍada; having arrived, he took his seat.

At that time, the maiden Sumati emerged from her quiet chamber; she first prostrated and knelt before her parents, and afterwards prostrated and knelt before the elder Pūrṇa, before returning to her quiet chamber.
At that time, the elder Pūrṇa, seeing the maiden Sumati, whose countenance was as beautiful as the color of a peach blossom and rare in this world, asked the elder Anāthapiṇḍada:
"Whose daughter is she?"
Anāthapiṇḍada replied,
"The woman you saw just now is my own daughter.
The elder Pūrṇa said:
"I have a young son who has not yet been married; could you provide a wife from a poor family?
At that time, the elder Anāthapiṇḍada replied, "This matter is not appropriate."
The householder Pūrṇa said:
"For what reason is it inappropriate?
Is it because of our lineage and reputation?"
"Is it because of wealth and property?
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada replied, "In terms of lineage and wealth, we are well-matched; however, the deity you worship is different from mine."
"This girl serves the Buddha, a disciple of Śākyamuni; you serve external paths and heterodox teachings. For this reason, she does not comply with your request.
Then the elder Pūrṇa said, "That which we serve, we shall naturally offer our own sacrifices for; that which this girl serves, she herself shall provide her own offerings for."
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada said:
"If my daughter were to marry into your family, the precious treasures she would bring would be beyond measure, and you, householder, would likewise have to provide treasures beyond measure."
The householder Pūrṇa said,
"How much wealth do you now demand?
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada replied:
"I now require sixty thousand ounces of gold.
At that time, the elder Pūrṇa immediately gave him sixty thousand ounces of gold.
Then, the elder Anāthapiṇḍada again had this thought:
"I have used skillful means to delay her, yet I am still unable to make her stop.
He said to the elder:
"If I were to give my daughter in marriage, I would first go to consult the Buddha; whatever instructions the World-Honored One may give, I shall carry them out."

At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika, having made an excuse as if he had some minor business to attend to, went out his door and proceeded to where the World-Honored One was; there he bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet in salutation and stood to one side.
At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"The daughter Sumati has been sought by the householder Pūrṇa of the city of Pūrṇamukha; may she be given to him?"
"Would it not be appropriate?
The World-Honored One replied,
"If the maiden Śyāmāvatī were to marry into that kingdom, she would bring immeasurable benefit and deliver countless people."
At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada again thought to himself:
"The World-Honored One, through his skillful means, knows that he should go to that land.

Then, the householder prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and withdrew to depart. Returning to his home, he prepared various kinds of delicious food and drink for the householder Pūrṇa.
The householder Pūrṇabhadra said, "What shall I do with this food? Will you simply give your daughter to me?
Anāthapiṇḍada replied:
"If you wish it so, you may follow my advice: have your son come here fifteen days from now.
Having said this, he withdrew and departed.

At that time, the elder Pūrṇa prepared the necessary provisions and set out in a carriage adorned with feathered ornaments, traveling from within eighty *yojanas*. The elder Anāthapiṇḍada, having likewise adorned his daughter, bathed her, perfumed her with incense, and placed her in a carriage adorned with feathered ornaments, went to meet the son of the elder Pūrṇa; they encountered one another midway.
When the period was full, Dhanapāla obtained a daughter and took her away to the city of Pūrṇabhadda.
At that time, the people of Pūrṇabhadda had established a regulation:
"If any woman in this city marries into another country, she shall be severely punished."
"Furthermore, if anyone from another country marries a wife and brings her into the kingdom, they shall likewise be subject to severe punishment.
At that time, there were six thousand brahmins in that country who were venerated by the people.
There was a restriction that stated:
"Should one violate the rule, one must provide a meal for six thousand brahmins.
At that time, the householder realized he had violated the rule and immediately provided a meal for six thousand brahmins.
However, the food consumed by these brahmins consists of roasted pork, pork soup, and heavily fermented wine;

furthermore, the clothing worn by these brahmins includes either white cotton cloth or woolen garments. Yet, according to the custom of those brahmins when entering a kingdom, they drape their robes over the right shoulder, leaving half the body exposed.
At that time, the householder immediately announced:
"The hour has come; the food and drink are prepared.
Thereupon, the six thousand brahmins, all wearing their robes over one shoulder with half their bodies exposed, entered the householder’s home.

At that time, seeing the brahmins approaching, the elder crawled forward on his knees to meet them and paid them respectful homage. The senior brahmin raised his hand in greeting, saying, "Excellent! He went forward, embraced the elder around the neck, and led him to his seat; the other brahmins each sat down according to their rank.
At that time, when the six thousand brahmins had finished taking their seats, the elder said to the maiden Sumati:
"Adorn yourself and pay homage to our teachers."
The maiden Sumati replied,
"Stop, stop, my lady!
I am not able to pay homage to those who are naked."
The elder said, "This is not a naked person, nor is he without a sense of shame; it is simply that the garment he wears is his dharma-robe. Sumati said:
"These shameless and unashamed people all expose their bodies together in public; what use do they have for religious robes?

Elder, please listen: the World-Honored One has also taught that there are two causes and conditions by which people of the world are esteemed, namely, having a sense of shame (*hrī*) and a sense of dread (*apatrāpya*)."

If these two matters did not exist, then parents, brothers, clans, and the five types of close relatives could not be distinguished by their status as superior or inferior, high or low; they would all belong to the same category without distinction of rank, like chickens, dogs, pigs, sheep, donkeys, and mules. Because these two principles exist in the world, there is an order of honor and subordination.
"However, these people, being devoid of these two qualities, herd together with chickens, dogs, pigs, sheep, donkeys, and mules; they are truly unfit to receive our prostrations.
Then the husband of Sūmā said to his wife:
"You should now rise and pay homage to our teachers; all these men are the deities whom I serve."
The woman Sumati replied: "Stop, noble son!
I cannot bring myself to pay homage to such shameless, naked men; by doing so, I would be paying homage to donkeys and dogs."
The husband spoke again, saying:
"Stop, stop!
Noble lady, do not speak such words. Guard your mouth and do not commit an offense; this is neither a donkey nor a madman, but the robe he wears is truly a Dharma-robe."
At that time, Sumati wept with tears streaming down her face; her complexion changed as she spoke these words:
"My parents and five kinsmen would rather have their bodies mangled by the fivefold mutilation and their life-faculties severed than ever fall into wrong views."
Then six thousand brahmins, each raising their voices together, spoke thus:
"Stop, stop!
Householder!"
"Why did this maidservant revile you so?
If you had requested us, we would have prepared the food and drink at that time.
Thereupon, the elder and the husband of Sūmātikā immediately prepared pork, pork stew, and heavily fermented wine, providing sufficient food for all six thousand brahmins.
After the brahmins had finished eating, they engaged in some discussion and then rose to depart.
At that time, the elder Pūrṇa was sitting alone on his high tower, distressed and lamenting as he reflected:
"Now that I have brought this girl here, I have ruined my household; it is no different from bringing disgrace upon my family."
At that time, there was a brahmin named Subhadra who had attained the five supernormal powers as well as the various dhyānas; he was highly esteemed by the elder Pūrṇa.
Then the brahmin Subhadra thought to himself:
"It has been a long time since I last saw the elder; I should go now to visit him."
At that time, the brahmin entered the city of Pūrṇa and went to the house of the elder, asking the gatekeeper:
"Where is the elder now?"
The gatekeeper replied, "The householder is upstairs, suffering from such extreme grief that it is beyond description.
Thereupon, the brahmin went straight up to the upper floor and met with the householder. The brahmin asked the householder:
"Why have you come to such a state of grief and anxiety?
Have you not been wronged by government officials, thieves, or calamities such as fire or water?
Is there some discord within your household?"
The elder replied, "There have been no disturbances from government officials or thieves; it is simply that the minor affairs of my household have not been successful.
The brahmin asked:
“I wish to hear the details; what were the circumstances?

The elder replied, “Yesterday, while I was marrying off my son, he violated the royal decree and brought disgrace upon our five kinsmen. I invited the Master to my house and intended to take my son’s bride there to pay her respects, but she did not obey my command.”
The brahmin Subhadra replied, "In which country does this girl's family reside? Is she near or far away for me to go and marry her?
The elder said:
"This woman is Anāthapiṇḍada’s daughter from the city of Śrāvastī.
When the brahmin Subhadra heard these words, he was filled with pity and astonishment; covering his ears with both hands, he spoke thus:
"Alas, alas, householder!
"How extraordinary! How marvelous!
That this woman was able to remain alive, neither taking her own life nor throwing herself from the tower below—this is truly a great fortune! Why is this so?"
"The teachers this girl serves are all practitioners of the holy life (brahmacarya) who are present here today; they are truly marvelous and extraordinary!
The elder said, "Having heard your words, I wish to mock you once more."
Why is this so? You are a follower of external paths and heterodox teachings; for what reason do you praise the conduct of the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākya?
What majestic power does the teacher whom this woman serves possess, and what supernatural transformations does he manifest?
The brahmin replied, "Householder!
Do you wish to hear of this girl’s spiritual virtues as a teacher?"
"I shall now briefly explain its source.
The elder said,
"I wish to hear this explanation."
The brahmin replied:
"In the past, I went among the people north of the Snowy Mountains to beg for food; having obtained food, I flew here to the Anavatapta Spring."
At that time, those devas, nāgas, and spirits saw me coming from afar; they all took up swords and spears and came toward me, saying to me in unison:
"O Rishi Subhadra!"
"Do not come to stop by this spring; do not defile this spring! If you do not follow my words, your life-force shall be severed right now.
Hearing these words, I immediately left that spring and ate at no great distance from it.

"Elder, you should know that the youngest disciple of this woman’s teacher, a novice named Kunda, has also gone to the north of the Snowy Mountains to beg for food. He flew to the Anavatapta Spring, where he stood with palms joined in reverence by a burial mound; there, his robes were stained with the blood and grime of the deceased."
At that time, the great devas, nāgas, spirits, and deities of Lake Anavatapta all rose to meet him, greeting him with reverence and asking after his well-being:
"Welcome, Teacher of Men!
Please be seated here."
Then the novice Saṃtuṣita went to the place where the spring was.

Furthermore, in the center of the spring, there was a table made of pure gold. At that time, the novice took the clothes of the deceased and soaked them in the water; afterwards, he sat down to eat. Having finished eating, he rinsed his bowl and sat cross-legged upon the golden table. Straightening his body and composing his mind, he focused his mindfulness before him and entered the first dhyāna.
Rising from the first dhyāna, he enters the second dhyāna; rising from the second dhyāna, he enters the third dhyāna;
rising from the third dhyāna, he enters the fourth dhyāna; rising from the fourth dhyāna, he enters the sphere of infinite space;

rising from the sphere of infinite space, he enters the sphere of infinite consciousness; rising from the sphere of infinite consciousness, he enters the sphere of nothingness; rising from the sphere of nothingness—
Entering the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he emerges from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and enters the samādhi of cessation;
emerging from the samādhi of cessation, he enters the samādhi of fiery radiance; emerging from the samādhi of fiery radiance, he enters the samādhi of watery vapor;
emerging from the samādhi of watery vapor, he enters the samādhi of fiery radiance once more, and subsequently enters cessation again.
Having exhausted the samādhi, he next enters the samādhi of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; next, he enters the samādhi of the sphere of nothingness;
next, he enters the samādhi of the sphere of infinite consciousness; next, he enters the samādhi of the sphere of infinite space;
next, he enters the fourth dhyāna; next, he enters the third dhyāna; next, he enters the second dhyāna; next, he enters...
In the first dhyāna, he rises from the first dhyāna to wash the clothes of a dead person.
At that time, devas, nāgas, and spirits either trample the clothes, or sprinkle water upon them, or take the water to drink.

At that time, having finished washing the robes, he lifted them up into the air to dry them; then, having gathered the robes together, the śrāmaṇera flew up into the air and returned to his dwelling place.

"Elder, you should know that at that time I saw her from afar but could not approach; if even the youngest disciple of this woman’s teacher possesses such supernormal power, how much more so must it be for the eldest disciple—what could possibly compare to him?"
How much less could one possibly reach that Teacher—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha?
Having contemplated this meaning, he made this statement: "How marvelous! How extraordinary!"
"How is it that this girl was able to do so without taking her own life or severing the life-faculty?
At that time, the elder said to the brahmin,
"May we be permitted to see the teacher whom this girl serves?"
The brahmin replied,
"You may ask this girl. Thereupon,
the elder questioned the maiden Sumati:
"I now wish to see the teacher whom you serve; can you cause him to come?
When the woman heard this, she was filled with such joy and exultation that she could not contain herself, and she said:
"Please prepare food and drink at once; tomorrow the Tathāgata and his community of bhikṣus shall come here."
The elder replied, "You have now requested it yourself; I do not understand the Dharma.
At that time, the elder’s daughter bathed her body, took incense and lamps in her hands, ascended to the upper story of the high tower, joined her palms toward the Tathāgata, and spoke these words:
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will examine this well; for none are able to see the crown of Your head.
Yet, World-Honored One, there is nothing You do not know and nothing You do not perceive. This woman now stands here in distress; may the World-Honored One examine her well.”
He further recited these verses:
"Observing the world without exception, That which is scrutinized by the Buddha-eye,
The various ghost kings have been subdued, As well as the Mother of Ghosts."
Just as that man-eating demon, who took human fingers to make a garland and later sought to harm his own mother, was nevertheless subdued by the Buddha;
and again, when a violent elephant in the city of Rājagṛha was about to come and do harm—
Furthermore, as for taking refuge, the various devas exclaimed, "Excellent!
He then went to the realm of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and encountered an evil dragon king;
upon seeing the Mārṣa Guhyapada, the dragon himself took refuge.
The various transformations are beyond reckoning, yet all are made to stand in the Right Path;
now that I have encountered this calamity, I pray only that the Honored One will deign to bend his divine power.
At that time, fragrances like clouds hung suspended in the midst of space.
Pervading the entire Jeta Grove, they stood before the Tathāgata.
All the Śākyas in the air paid homage to the Buddha with joy;
they also saw the incense before them, which had been offered by Sumati.
Various kinds of flowers rained down, beyond all measure, completely filling the Jeta Grove as the Tathāgata smiled and emitted light.

At that time, Ānanda perceived this wondrous fragrance within the Jeta Grove; having seen it, he went to the place where the World-Honored One was, and upon arrival, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and stood to one side.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I pray, World-Honored One!
What kind of fragrance is this that pervades the entirety of the Jeta Grove Monastery?"
The World-Honored One said:
"This incense is sent by the Buddha; it was requested by the woman Sumati in the city of Pūrṇa.
Now you must summon all the bhikṣus to assemble in one place and distribute voting sticks, issuing this command:”

"Whichever bhikṣus who are arhats with exhausted outflows and have attained the supernormal powers take up their requisites, for tomorrow they shall go to the city of Pūrṇa to accept the invitation of Sumati."
Ānanda said to the Buddha, “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
At that time, having received the Buddha’s instruction, Ānanda immediately gathered the bhikṣus in the Hall of Universal Assembly and thought to himself:
"All those who have attained the path as arhats must take their robes and bowls; tomorrow we shall go to accept the invitation of Sumati."

At that time, there was a senior monk among the assembly named Kuṇḍadhāna who had attained the stage of *srotāpanna*. Although his fetters (*saṃyojana*) were not yet exhausted, he had not attained the supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*). Then the senior monk thought to himself:

"I am the most senior among this great assembly; yet, as my fetters are not yet exhausted and I have not attained the supernormal powers, I will not be able to reach the city of Pūrṇa for the midday meal tomorrow."

"However, among the assembly of the Tathāgata, the one seated at the lowest rank is the novice Śramaṇera named Cunda; he possesses supernormal powers and great majestic might, and is able to go there to accept the invitation. I, too, shall now go to accept that invitation."
At that time, the Elder, with a mind purified, while still abiding in the stage of training, received the voting tally (*śalākā*).

Then, with his purified divine eye, the World-Honored One saw that Kuṇḍopadhānīya, who was abiding in the stage of training, had received the tally and attained the state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Among my disciples, the one foremost in receiving śalākā [voting sticks] is the bhikṣu Kuṇṭhapanthaka."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus with supernormal powers:
"Mahāmaudgalyāyana! Mahākāśyapa!"
Ānanda! Revata! Subhūti!
Upavikaśyapa! Mahāpiṇḍola!
Venerable Rāhula!
"Equanimous Benefactor! Half-Holder!
Equanimous Head! Śrāmaṇeras, you shall go first by means of your supernormal powers to that city."
The bhikṣus replied,
“So be it, World-Honored One! At that time,
the Saṃgha appointed a man named Gaṇḍaka, who early the next morning personally carried a large cauldron, flew through the air, and went to that city.
At that time, the elder and the people climbed to the top of a high tower, wishing to behold the World-Honored One. From afar, they saw a messenger coming along, carrying a cauldron on his back.
Then the elder and his daughter spoke this verse:
"Clad in white garments with long hair, His body exposed like a swift wind."
Furthermore, she was carrying a large cauldron on her back. [The Buddha asked: "Is this your teacher?
At that time, the woman replied with a verse:
"This is not your noble disciple; he is an envoy of the Tathāgata."
"One who possesses the three tools and the five supernormal powers is called a *khaṇḍa*.
At that time, the *khaṇḍa* sent a messenger to circle the city three times before proceeding to the house of the elder.

At that time, the śrāmaṇera Śunahotra manifested five hundred flowering trees of various colors, all of them in full bloom; their colors were exceedingly beautiful, like those of the utpala lotus. Such flowers were beyond measure as he proceeded toward that city.
At that time, the elder saw the śrāmaṇera approaching from afar and again asked him in verse:
"These various kinds of flowers, All suspended in the midst of space—
Is there a person with supernormal powers Who is your teacher?"
At that time, the woman replied with a verse:
"Regarding Subhadra’s previous statement about the śrāmaṇera by the spring:
his teacher was named Śāriputra, and he was that man’s disciple."
At that time, the novice Saṃgharakṣita circumambulated the city three times and proceeded to the house of the elder.
At that same moment, the Venerable Pūrṇa manifested five hundred oxen, all with blue coats and hair; he sat cross-legged upon them and traveled toward that city.
At that time, the elder saw her from afar and again questioned the girl with this verse:
"These great herds of cattle, Their coats all blue in color, Upon them you sit alone; Is this your teacher?"
The woman replied with a verse:
"He who can transform a thousand bhikṣus within the grove at the city of Śrāvastī,
whose mind and spirit are exceedingly clear— this one is named Paṇḍita."
At that time, the Venerable Cūḷapanthaka, having circumambulated that city three times, proceeded to the house of the elder.
At that same time, Rāhula again manifested five hundred peacocks of various colors; seated cross-legged upon them, he proceeded toward that city.
Having seen this, the elder again addressed the girl with these verses:
"These five hundred peacocks, Their colors are most wondrous;
Like those great generals of an army, Are these your teachers?"
Then the woman replied with this verse:
“The Tathāgata has taught the prohibitions and precepts, that one must not transgress anything at all;
he who can guard the precepts within the precepts is the Buddha’s son, Rāhula.”
At that time, Rāhula circumambulated the city three times and proceeded to the house of the elder.
At that same moment, the Venerable Kapphiṇa transformed himself into five hundred extremely powerful garuḍas; sitting cross-legged upon them, he traveled toward that city.
At that time, having seen her from afar, the elder again addressed the girl with this verse:
“Five hundred garuḍas, Extremely powerful and courageous,
Fearless as they soar above— Are these your teachers?”
Then the woman replied with a verse:
"One who can practice the inhalation and exhalation, who turns the mind toward wholesome conduct,
and whose power of wisdom is exceedingly fierce— this one is called a Kappina."
Then the Venerable Kapphiṇa circumambulated the city three times and proceeded to the house of the householder.
At that time, Upaka-Kāśyapa manifested five hundred seven-headed nāgas, sitting cross-legged upon them, as he proceeded toward that city.
Having seen them from afar, the elder again addressed the girl with this verse:
"These seven-headed dragons, Their majestic countenances are most fearsome;
Those who come are beyond counting— Are these your teachers?"
At that time, the woman replied:
"He who always has a thousand disciples, who transforms Vaiśravaṇa through his supernormal powers,
and who is Upakaśyapa— of him one may say he is this man."
At that time, Upaka-Kāśyapa circumambulated the city three times and proceeded to the house of the elder.
At that moment, the Venerable Subhūti manifested a mountain of lapis lazuli, entered it, sat down cross-legged, and traveled toward that city.
At that time, having seen her from afar, the elder addressed the girl in verse, saying:
"This mountain is most wondrous, Entirely the color of lapis lazuli;
Now sitting within this cave— Is this your teacher?"
Then the woman replied with this verse:
"By virtue of the retribution for a single past gift, I have now obtained this merit;
Having become a fertile field of blessings, I am Subhūti, who understands emptiness."
At that time, Subhūti circumambulated the city three times and proceeded to the house of the elder.
Then the Venerable Mahākātyāyana, having again manifested as five hundred geese, all pure white in color, went toward that city.
At that time, the elder saw them from afar and asked the girl in verse:
"These five hundred cranes, All of their colors pure white,
Filling the entirety of space— Are these your teachers?"
Then the woman replied with this verse:
“The Buddha’s discourses explain, Analyzing their meanings and phrases, And further expounding upon the mass of fetters; This is named Kaccāyana.”
At that time, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana circumambulated the city three times and proceeded to the house of the elder.
At that same time, Revata manifested five hundred tigers and went to that city, sitting atop them as he traveled.
Having seen this, the elder questioned the girl with these verses:
"These five hundred tigers, Their fur and coats are so very bright and joyful;
And he who sits upon them— Is he your teacher?"
Then the woman replied with a verse:
"Formerly at the Jeta Grove, for six years he did not move;
supreme in seated meditation, this one is named Revata."
At that time, the Venerable Revata circumambulated the city three times and proceeded to the house of the householder.
At that same time, the Venerable Aniruddha manifested five hundred lions of extreme ferocity and went to that city, sitting atop them.
At that time, having seen this, the elder questioned the girl with a verse:
"These five hundred lions are so fierce and terrifying;
is he who sits upon them your teacher?"
Then the woman replied with a verse:
"At the time of his birth, the earth shook greatly, and precious jewels emerged from the ground.
With pure eyes free from defilement, he is the Buddha’s younger brother, Aniruddha."
At that time, Aniruddha circumambulated the city three times and proceeded to the house of the elder.

At that same time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa manifested five hundred horses, all with vermilion manes and tails adorned with interlaced gold and silver; seated upon them, he rained down celestial flowers as he proceeded toward that city.
Having seen them from afar, the elder questioned the girl in verse:
"Five hundred golden horses with vermilion tails—
are these the wheels-turning kings?"
"Is he your teacher?
The woman replied again in verse:
"He is foremost in the practice of *dhūta*, And ever compassionate toward the poor."
"The Tathāgata shared half his seat with him; he was Mahākāśyapa.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa circumambulated the city three times and proceeded to the house of the elder.

At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana manifested five hundred elephants, each with six tusks, their seven parts well-proportioned and adorned with interlaced gold and silver. Seated upon them, they emitted great radiance that filled the entire world as they approached the city through the air. There, amidst the sky, they performed an incalculable array of musical performances and offered rains of various kinds of flowers; furthermore, within the sky, suspended silk banners and canopies were most wondrous and marvelous.
At that time, having seen him from afar, the elder questioned the girl with a verse:
"A white elephant with six tusks, Seated above like a celestial king;
Now hearing the sound of music, Is this Śākyamuni?"
Then the woman replied with a verse:
"On that great mountain, he who has subdued the Nanda Dragon and is foremost in supernormal powers is named Mahāmaudgalyāyana."
"My teacher has not yet arrived; these are his disciples.
The noble teacher shall now come, and there is no place his radiance does not illuminate.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana circumambulated the city three times and proceeded to the house of the elder.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the hour had come, donned his saṃghāṭī robe and ascended into the air at a height of seven *zhú* above the ground.

At that moment, Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya stood to the right of the Tathāgata, and Śāriputra stood to his left; meanwhile, Ānanda, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, followed behind the Tathāgata holding a fly-whisk, while twelve hundred disciples surrounded him from front and back.

The Tathāgata was situated at the very center. Among his disciples possessed of supernatural powers (*ṛddhipāda*), Ājñātakauṇḍinya manifested as the Moon Deva-son, and Śāriputra manifested as the Sun Deva-son. The other monks endowed with supernatural powers some manifested as Śakra-devendra, some as Brahmā, some as the forms of Dhṛtarāṣṭra or Virūḍhaka, and some as Virūpākṣa or Vaiśravaṇa leading hosts of spirits and deities; others manifested as the form of a Wheel-Turning Sage King (*cakravartin*).
Some entered the Fire-Light Samādhi, some entered the Water-Crystal Samādhi, some emitted light, and some emitted smoke, performing various kinds of supernatural feats.

At that time, Brahmā, King of the Gods, stood to the right of the Tathāgata; Śakra, Lord of the Devas, stood to the left of the Tathāgata holding a fly-whisk; Guhyapāda, the Vajrapāṇi Māravijayin, stood behind the Tathāgata holding a vajra; and Vaiśravaṇa, King of the Gods, stood in the air above the Tathāgata holding a canopy of the seven precious gems, fearing that dust might fall upon the body of the Tathāgata.

At that time, Pañcaśikha held a lapis lazuli lute in his hand and extolled the merits of the Tathāgata; meanwhile, all the celestial deities in the midst of the void performed tens of millions of kinds of musical performances, raining down various celestial flowers scattered upon the Tathāgata.

At that time, King Prasenajit, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, and the people of Śrāvastī all saw the Tathāgata in the air, seven fathoms above the ground; having seen him, they were all filled with joy and leaped for gladness, unable to contain themselves.
At that time, the elder Anāthapiṇḍada spoke this verse:
“The Tathāgata is truly divine and wondrous; He loves the people as if they were his own infants.
How joyful is Sumati! He shall receive the Dharma of the Tathāgata.”

At that time, King Prasenajit and the householder Anāthapiṇḍada scattered various kinds of named incenses and miscellaneous flowers. Then the World-Honored One, surrounded by the assembly of bhikṣus before and behind, as well as by innumerable devas and spirits, proceeded toward that city through the air like a king of geese.
At that time, Pañcaśikha praised the Buddha with these verses:
"All fetters of birth are forever exhausted; His mental intentions are neither confused nor distracted.
With dust and defilement stilled, he has reached fulfillment; He enters that ancient realm."
The nature of his mind is utterly pure, having severed all demonic and evil thoughts;
with merit as vast as the great ocean, he now enters that land.
His countenance is most extraordinary, and no afflictions shall ever arise again.
Because he does not abide for himself, he now enters that land;
having crossed the abyss of the four torrents, he has escaped birth, old age, and death;
having severed the root-source of existence, he now enters that land.

At that time, the elder Pūrṇa saw from afar the World-Honored One approaching; his faculties were serene and rare in the world, as pure as celestial gold. His body was adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, appearing like Mount Sumeru rising above all other mountains, or like a mass of gold emitting a great radiance.
At that time, the elder questioned Sumati with these verses:
"Is this the light of the sun? Never before have I seen such a countenance.
Amidst these many thousands of millions of rays, I do not dare to gaze upon it intently."
At that time, the maiden Sumati knelt with palms joined toward the Tathāgata and replied to the elder in verse:
"He is neither the sun nor possessed of the sun, yet he emits a thousand kinds of light.
For the sake of all sentient beings, he is likewise my teacher."
"All together they praise the Tathāgata, as previously described;
now we shall surely obtain the great fruit—let us diligently increase our offerings.
At that time, the elder Pūrṇadhana knelt with his right knee on the ground and again praised the Tathāgata in verse, saying:
“I take refuge in the Honored One of Ten Powers, whose body is of golden hue and radiant light, praised and revered by devas and humans; today I surrender my life to him.
The Honored One is now the King of the Day, as bright as the moon among the stars.”
Having delivered those not yet delivered, today I take refuge in you.
Like the image of the Lord of Devas, like one who practices the Brahma-conduct with a compassionate heart,
having liberated yourself and delivering all sentient beings, today I take refuge in you.
"Honored One among gods and men, supreme above all ghost-king deities,
you who have subdued all non-Buddhists— to you I now take refuge. At that time,
the maiden Sumati knelt with palms joined and praised the World-Honored One, saying:
"Having subdued oneself, one can subdue others; having ceased oneself, one causes others to cease.
By means of deliverance, one delivers the people; having attained liberation, one liberates others.
Having crossed to the other shore, one enables others to cross; having illuminated oneself, one illuminates the multitude of beings."
There is nothing that lacks measure; removing strife, there is no contention or dispute.
Abiding in ultimate purity, the mind does not waver.
Out of compassion for the world, the One of Ten Powers is honored with prostrations from my head.

"Possessing the minds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; endowed with emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; most honored and foremost within the desire realm; supreme among the devas; fully possessing the seven riches; protecting gods and humans through the spontaneous birth of Brahmā; peerless and beyond compare—today I take refuge in him."
At that time, six thousand brahmins, seeing the World-Honored One perform such a supernatural transformation, each said to one another:
"We should leave this country and go to other lands; this śramaṇa Gautama has already subdued the people of this kingdom."

At that time, the six thousand brahmins immediately departed from the kingdom and never entered it again; they were like the lion, king of beasts, who emerges from the mountain valleys, surveys the four quarters, and lets out three roars before proceeding on its quest.

All classes of beasts and insects each fled toward their respective destinations, not knowing where to go; whether flying away, fleeing, or sinking into hiding—just as when powerful, divine elephants hear the roar of a lion, they each flee toward their own quarters, unable to remain at ease.
Why is this so? It is because the lion, king of beasts, possesses supreme majesty and spiritual power; this case is likewise.
When those six thousand brahmins heard the sound of the World-Honored One’s voice, they each fled in haste, unable to find peace.
Why was this so? It was because of the spiritual power possessed by the śramaṇa Gautama.
At that time, the World-Honored One withdrew his supernormal powers and entered the city of Pūrṇavardhana according to his usual custom.
At that time, as the World-Honored One stepped upon the threshold of the gate, heaven and earth shook greatly, and the various honored deities scattered flowers as an offering.
At that time, the people beheld the World-Honored One’s countenance and faculties in a state of profound stillness, adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics.
The people then spoke this verse:
“The Most Honored among Two-Legged Beings is supremely wondrous; Even a brahmin would not dare to equal him.
There is no need to serve a brahmin; One has lost this Honored One among Men.”
At that time, the World-Honored One went to the house of the elder and sat upon the prepared seat.

At that moment, the people of that country were extremely numerous; there were eighty-four thousand people from the elder’s household who had all gathered like clouds, intending to demolish the elder’s residence. Just as they were about to do so, they beheld the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus.

Thereupon, the World-Honored One thought to himself: "These people will surely suffer injury. I should exercise my supernatural power so that all the people of the entire kingdom may see my body and the community of bhikṣus."

At that time, the World-Honored One transformed the house of the elder so that it became the color of lapis lazuli, transparent inside and out, as if one were looking at a jewel in the palm of one’s hand.
Then, the girl Sumati approached the Buddha, prostrated herself with her head at his feet, and with a heart filled with both grief and joy, she spoke this verse:
“Possessing all wisdom, You have fully transcended all dharmas.”
Furthermore, having severed the net of desire and craving, I now take refuge in you.
I would rather have my parents destroy both my eyes than come to this place among those of wrong views and the five heinous crimes.
"What evil conditions did I create in my past lives, that I have come to this place like a bird caught in a net? I pray that you will sever these knots of doubt.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to the woman in verse:
"Do not now worry at all; let your mind be serene and open.
Do not give rise to conceptual attachments, for the Tathāgata shall now expound [the Dharma].
You originally had no karmic conditions for sin, yet you have been able to come to this place."
By the fruit of my vow and resolve, I desire to deliver these sentient beings.
Now I shall uproot their very source so they do not fall into the three evil realms;
thousands of classes of sentient beings shall attain liberation before you.
"Today you shall purify yourself and attain the eye of wisdom;
may the gods and the people of this world see you as one beholds a precious gem.
When the maiden Sumati heard these words, she was filled with such joy and exultation that she could not contain herself.

At that time, the elder, together with his attendants, provided various kinds of delicious food and drink. Seeing that the World-Honored One had finished eating, he offered pure water and took another small seat to sit before the Tathāgata. His followers and the eighty-four thousand members of the assembly each sat down in their respective order; some sat while announcing their own names.

At that time, the World-Honored One gradually delivered a sublime discourse to the elder and the eighty-four thousand people of his kind. This discourse consisted of teachings on morality, teachings on generosity, and teachings on rebirth in heaven; it explained that sensual desires are impure, that outflows are defilements and evils, and that renouncing the household life is the essential path.

At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing that the minds of the elder, the girl Sumati, and the eighty-four thousand people had been opened and their intentions liberated, proclaimed to all these sentient beings the Dharma that all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, constantly teach: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Each of them, upon their seats, was cleansed of all defilements and attained the pure Dharma-eye; just as an extremely pure white woolen cloth is easily dyed with color, so it was with them.

The elder Pūrṇa, the maiden Sumati, and the eighty-four thousand people among their kind all cleansed themselves of every defilement and attained the purity of the Dharma-eye; free from further doubt, they gained fearlessness and all took refuge in the Triple Gem and undertook the five precepts.
At that time, the maiden Sumati spoke these verses before the Buddha:
“The Tathāgata’s ears are pure and clear; Hearing that I have encountered this suffering, He has descended his spirit to this place to transform me, So that all people may attain the Dharma-eye.”
At that time, when the World-Honored One had finished preaching the Dharma, he rose from his seat and returned to his dwelling.
Then, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By what causes and conditions was the girl Sumati born into a wealthy and noble family in her previous life?"
By what causes and conditions did he fall into a family that holds such wrong views?
By what wholesome merits did he now attain the purity of the Dharma-eye?
And by what merits did he cause eighty-four thousand people to all attain the purity of the Dharma-eye?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"In the distant past, during this Bhadrakalpa, there was a Buddha named Kāśyapa—a teacher perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader of persons, a trainer of the path of Dharma, a teacher of gods and humans, called a Buddha and a Blessed One—who was wandering and teaching within the borders of the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, together with a great assembly of twenty thousand bhikṣus."

At that time, there was a king named Karuṇā (Compassion) who had a daughter named Sumana. At that time, this girl possessed the utmost reverence; she upheld the prohibitive precepts before the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, constantly delighted in practicing generosity, and furthermore provided the fourfold offerings.
What are the four? First, giving; second, affectionate respect; third, benefiting others; and fourth, impartial benefit.
At the abode of Tathāgata Kāśyapa, he recited the Dharma-verses from atop a high tower, chanting them aloud and making this aspiration:

"Since these four dharmas of love have been constantly present, and since I have recited these Dharma verses before the Tathāgata, if there be even a hair’s breadth of merit therein, may I not fall into the evil realms nor be born into a poor household wherever I am reborn. In future lives, may I likewise encounter such a World-Honored One as this, and may I never again turn back into a woman's body; rather, while still in this female body, may I attain the purity of the Dharma-eye."

At that time, the people of the city, hearing that the princess had made such a vow, all gathered together and went to where the princess was, saying this: "Today the princess has practiced with the utmost sincerity, performing various meritorious deeds;

she has not lacked in the four requisites, practicing generosity while simultaneously benefiting others through love and impartiality. She has further made a vow to encounter such a Honored One in a future life, so that if he preaches the Dharma for her, she may immediately attain the pure Dharma-eye. Today the princess has already made her vow; we pray that she and the people of our kingdom may all attain deliverance at the same time."
Then the princess replied, "I shall take this merit and bestow it upon you all;
should we encounter a Tathāgata preaching the Dharma, he shall deliver you all simultaneously."
"O Bhikṣu! How could there be any doubt?
Do not hold such a view."
The King of Compassion at that time was the elder Sudatta;
the king’s daughter at that time was the maiden Sumati;
and the people of that land were the present assembly of eighty-four thousand.
By virtue of that vow, they have now encountered my person, heard the Dharma, and attained the Way; furthermore, all those among the populace have completely purified their Dharma-eye.
This is its meaning; you should reflect upon it and practice accordingly.
Why is this so? Because these four matters are the supreme fields of merit.
If there is a bhikṣu who draws near to these four matters, he shall attain the Four Truths; he should therefore seek skillful means to accomplish the dharma of these four matters.
"Thus, O bhikṣus,
you should train yourselves.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Sūtra of the Girl Sumati
